stories.headline: FAA Outage Update: two aviation outages in four days, officials say no cyberattack
stories.summary: This is an update on Friday's nationwide ground stop, which Briefed led with on Nov. 14, and on a separate United Airlines outage on Monday. The Federal Aviation Administration says a telecommunications failure, including work on a new router, flooded its network. In a questions-and-answers post, the F.A.A. said its investigation pointed to a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris was deploying a new router; those sites were blocked and the new-router broadcast was disabled. "Based on all available evidence, we have no indication that this was a cyberattack or an outside nefarious actor," the F.A.A. said. The stop ran from about 3:30 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, Nov. 13, and about 3,500 airborne aircraft landed safely. Operators canceled about 12,462 flights that Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines; the F.A.A. said not all of those cancellations were caused by the ground stop. On Monday, Nov. 16, United Airlines said a technology issue delayed departing flights, with no impact on flights already in the air or on United Express, and that it had no indication it was a cybersecurity issue. The F.A.A. said that outage was a United technology problem, not an F.A.A. equipment issue. CNN, citing United spokesperson Leslie Scott, reported a disruption of about 30 minutes affecting fewer than 150 flights; the Associated Press described a longer disruption. The two events were not presented as connected. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has also said the Friday event did not appear to be a cyberattack.

quickFacts: Friday, Nov. 13: nationwide F.A.A. ground stop, about 3:30–8:15 p.m. ET
F.A.A.: a telecommunications failure, including work on a new router, flooded its network; no indication of a cyberattack
Monday, Nov. 16: a separate United Airlines systems outage delayed departures
United and the F.A.A. say the Monday outage was a United technology problem, not a cyberattack
notYetConfirmed: A final technical cause of Friday's failure, beyond the F.A.A.'s preliminary account of the router work and flooded network
A precise, official tally of how many Monday delays were caused by United's outage; CNN and the A.P. reported different durations
whatHappensNext: The F.A.A. investigation into Friday's ground stop is continuing
Travelers should check with their airline for the latest on delayed or canceled flights

stories.headline: Nvidia reports $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103%, and guides to $130 billion
stories.summary: Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday evening, its first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and 20% from the prior quarter, according to the company. Net income was $65.3 billion. Data-center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110%. For the current quarter, Nvidia guided to $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, and said it assumed no China data-center compute sales. The company also raised its growth outlook for the following year to 75%. Board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. Interim chief executive and chief financial officer Colette Kress remains in those roles. BBC reported that shares rose 4.8% after hours.

quickFacts: Q3 fiscal 2027 revenue: $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier (Nvidia)
This-quarter guide: $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%; no China data-center compute assumed
Board chair Harvey Jones: the board will not reinstate Jensen Huang
Shares rose 4.8% after hours (BBC)
notYetConfirmed: How long Colette Kress will remain interim chief executive, and who the board will name as a permanent C.E.O.
whatHappensNext: Investors will parse the call and the raised growth outlook
The board's C.E.O. search continues; it says it will not reinstate Huang

stories.headline: Trump lands in Shenzhen ahead of Thursday's meeting with Xi and Putin
stories.summary: President Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday for APEC meetings, ahead of a Thursday trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, according to CNBC and the Associated Press. The talks are expected to cover the Iran war, Ukraine and strategic stability. Reporting so far has described expectations for a concrete deal as low. A possible meeting with North Korea's Kim Jong Un has been floated; it has not been confirmed.

quickFacts: Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday for APEC
Thursday: expected meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin
Agenda expected to include the Iran war and Ukraine
Expectations for a concrete deal are low, according to the coverage
notYetConfirmed: Whether Trump will also meet Kim Jong Un; that has been floated, not confirmed
Whether Thursday's talks produce any announced agreement
whatHappensNext: The trilateral meeting is expected on Thursday
Watch for any readout on Iran, Ukraine or a broader deal

stories.headline: U.S. and Thailand announce a substantial conclusion of a reciprocal trade agreement
stories.summary: In Manila on Tuesday, President Trump and Thailand's prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, announced a "substantial conclusion" of an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, according to a White House joint statement. The statement said both governments "will now begin their respective necessary internal processes to prepare the ART for signature and entry into force." It is not a signed agreement and is not in force. The Hill also reported the announcement.

quickFacts: Announced Tuesday in Manila by President Trump and Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul
Described as a "substantial conclusion" of a reciprocal trade agreement (White House)
Both sides still have internal processes to finish before signature and entry into force
It is not a signed deal and is not in force
notYetConfirmed: The full text and detailed terms of the agreement
When the two sides will sign it and when it would enter into force
whatHappensNext: Each government begins its internal processes to prepare the agreement for signature
Signature and entry into force would come after those steps

stories.headline: Mary Peltola wins Alaska's Senate race, giving Democrats a 56-44 majority
stories.summary:
Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's U.S. Senate race, the last 2026 Senate seat called, defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. With about 99% of votes counted she had 50.1% of first-choice votes, so a ranked-choice tabulation was not needed, according to coverage of the Alaska Division of Elections count. The result projects a 56-44 Democratic majority in the Senate, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. NBC News called the race at 10:19 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday; the BBC also reported the result. Peltola would be the first Alaska Native U.S. senator and the first Democrat to win an Alaska Senate race since 2008. The incumbent's campaign has not conceded and said it would comment by the end of the week.

A second candidate with a similar name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., also appeared on the ballot. He is a retired elementary school teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, and he filed as a Republican under his legal name. Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher initially excluded him, concluding the filing was not a good-faith candidacy and was "filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead." He sued. Alaska Superior Court Judge Thomas A. Matthews ruled in June that the division had abused its discretion and relied on a "good-faith" requirement not in the state's constitution, statutes or regulations; the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed and ordered him onto the August primary ballot. He advanced from that primary. The New York Times reported in October that aides to Peltola's campaign and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee personnel helped recruit him to siphon votes. Peltola said she knew nothing about other candidates on the ballot except herself and the incumbent and that she was "not interested in tricking voters." Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has said he had no contact with her campaign — "Zero, none, zilch" — and that Sullivan is the name and party of his father and grandfather. Motives and any recruitment remain disputed. BBC Verify reported that even combining both Sullivans' first-choice votes would not have overtaken Peltola.

quickFacts: Peltola: 50.1% of first-choice votes with about 99% counted; last 2026 Senate seat called
Projected Senate: 56-44 Democratic majority, including two independents who caucus with Democrats
A second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, also ran
Officials first blocked him as meant to confuse voters; Alaska courts ordered him on the ballot
The New York Times reported people with Peltola's campaign helped recruit him; she said she knew nothing about it, and he has denied any contact with her campaign
The incumbent has not conceded
notYetConfirmed: Whether anyone in Peltola's campaign recruited the second Sullivan; the Times report is disputed by her denial and by his denial of any contact
Whether the incumbent will concede, or challenge the result, by the end of the week
whatHappensNext: The incumbent's campaign said it would comment by the end of the week
Peltola is expected to be seated in the new Senate

stories.headline: Haitians rally in support of Bukele and Salvadoran troops
stories.summary: Thousands of people marched Tuesday, Nov. 17, in Port-au-Prince and other cities in support of El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele and Salvadoran troops sent to Haiti to fight gangs, according to the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse. Al Jazeera, citing agency reporting, described crowds in several Haitian cities and, in one account, used the lower figure "hundreds." Signs included "Thank you, Bukele" and "Long live Bukele"; some marchers called for "drones and the dogs." In the afternoon in Port-au-Prince, police used tear gas as a march headed toward Sylvio-Cator stadium, which had recently been retaken. Bukele sent about 2,500 troops (A.P. and France 24 said some 2,500; A.F.P. has also said more than 2,000) after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing in an Oct. 18 ambush during a U.N.-backed Gang Suppression Force operation. The new surge is largely separate from that force: U.N. spokesman Stéphane Dujarric and later reporting have said only a few hundred of the Salvadoran personnel are under the U.N.-backed mission, with the rest operating under a bilateral Haiti–El Salvador arrangement. Haiti's government said Tuesday that its Council of Ministers approved a cooperation agreement; terms were not specified, and Salvadoran Vice President Félix Ulloa said Monday the bilateral agreement would not be made public. Salvadoran Security Minister Gustavo Villatoro said troops would leave once the missing airmen are found. Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pélissier, speaking in San Salvador, said Tuesday there was "no date" for them to leave and that officials would work on a legal framework to stay longer, at least until elections next year. On the U.S. role, Axios reported that Bukele called President Trump and that Trump told him to "do what you have to do," citing anonymous sources. Deutsche Welle later quoted Trump on the record: "He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: 'Look, you're running your country. You have to do what you have to do.'" Axios also reported that Bukele requested drones and transport and was officially denied, and that Trump said Bukele "doesn't need help." There has been no confirmed U.S. funding or U.S. troop role in this surge.

quickFacts: Tuesday, Nov. 17: thousands marched in Port-au-Prince and other cities (A.P., A.F.P.)
About 2,500 Salvadoran troops, sent by President Bukele, are in Haiti to fight gangs
Most of the troops operate outside the U.N.-backed Gang Suppression Force
Haiti's government said it approved a cooperation agreement Tuesday; terms were not published
Trump has said, on the record, that he told Bukele he had to "do what you have to do"; no confirmed U.S. funding or U.S. troops in the surge
notYetConfirmed: A precise crowd size; Al Jazeera also used "hundreds," below the "thousands" figure from A.P. and A.F.P.
The unpublished terms of the Haiti–El Salvador cooperation agreement, and how long the troops will stay (Salvadoran and Haitian officials have given different accounts)
Any U.S. logistical support beyond Trump's public comment; requests for drones and transport were officially denied, per Axios
whatHappensNext: The search for the four missing Salvadoran airmen continues
Haiti and El Salvador may publish, or keep private, the legal framework for the deployment
Whether the troops remain through Haiti's planned elections next year is unresolved

stories.whyItMattersToUS: President Trump has said he told El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, to 'do what you have to do' on Haiti; there is no confirmed U.S. funding or U.S. troop role in the surge.
